idiom_name: std::unique_ptr<Impl> with out-of-line destructor and moves
implementation_notes: The modern default: forward-declare the body in the header, hold it by std::unique_ptr, and define the destructor plus the move operations out of line in the .cpp where the body is complete - unique_ptr needs a complete type to delete, which is exactly why the out-of-line destructor is mandatory here. Declaring the move operations back (or defining them out of line as defaulted) keeps the handle a cheap movable value type instead of a copyable-but-stuck one, and per the Core Guidelines this is the form to reach for when a stable library ABI matters. Reach for the raw-pointer form only on pre-C++11 toolchains or when the ownership policy is genuinely custom.
pitfalls: A destructor (or copy/move operation) defaulted or defined in the header is instantiated in every client translation unit while the body is incomplete - the classic std::default_delete compile error, or a silently wrong ABI.
A user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move operations, so the handle silently becomes non-movable (and non-copyable); declare and define them explicitly.
Member functions cannot be inlined across the firewall, so hot accessors pay an out-of-line call plus a pointer indirection - keep those members visible or accept the cost deliberately.

variants.name: Fast pImpl (in-place aligned storage)
variants.idiom_name: alignas buffer + placement new + std::launder (Fast Pimpl)
variants.implementation_notes: Removes both costs of the classic form - the heap allocation and the pointer indirection - by embedding a fixed-size, correctly aligned buffer in the handle and constructing the body inside it, as described in GotW #28 and the More C++ Idioms Fast Pimpl chapter. A static_assert(sizeof(Impl) <= sizeof storage_) compiled in the implementation file turns a too-small buffer into a build error, and C++17 supplies std::launder to reach the object and std::destroy_at to destroy it (std::aligned_storage itself is deprecated in C++23; prefer alignas plus std::byte). Choose it only after profiling shows the allocation matters: the buffer size is now visible in the header, so the body can no longer grow without an ABI break, which forfeits a large part of the reason to use pimpl at all.
pitfalls: Size and alignment are guesses written in the header; different platforms or standard-library implementations can change sizeof(Impl), so the static_assert must be compiled on every target you ship and the buffer maintained by hand whenever the body grows.

Placement new plus explicit destruction means the lifetime of the object is your responsibility: exceptions during construction, copy/move of a non-bitwise-copyable buffer and std::launder misuse are undefined behaviour, not compile errors.

The fixed buffer is part of the interface, so this variant is for internal or already-ABI-frozen types; using it for a published library silently reintroduces exactly the layout dependency the classic pimpl removed.

variants.name: Hand-rolled pimpl with a raw pointer (C++03, rule of three)
variants.idiom_name: raw Impl* with hand-written destructor, copy constructor and assignment
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++11 form, still the only option on C++03 toolchains and the base of the Qt/KDE d-pointer style: a raw pointer member whose destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment are all written out of line - the bookkeeping that unique_ptr automates (the rule of three, or five once moves appear). It also expresses ownership policies the standard smart pointers do not, such as a fixed-size pool allocator for an object created in bulk, and it allows a deliberately valueless handle. Keep it for legacy targets or genuinely custom allocation; otherwise unique_ptr documents intent and is exception-safe by construction.
pitfalls: Rule-of-three drift: a forgotten copy constructor or assignment gives shallow aliases and double deletes, and exception safety has to be re-derived by hand (copy-and-swap) rather than coming from the smart pointer.
A raw pointer also permits a null body, so every member function must define what a valueless object does - or the constructor must guarantee a body and the class must document that invariant.
